When the number of hidden units is less than the number of inputs, the multilayer perceptron is trained to find the best coding of the inputs on the hidden units, performing dimensionality reduction. 1 1 .1 0   Autoencoders An interesting architecture is the autoencoder ( Cottrell, Munro, and Zipser 1 9 8 7 ) , which is an MLP architecture where there are as many outputs as there are inputs, and the required output is defined to be equal to the input ( see figure 1 1 .1 5 ) . When the number of hidden units is less than the number of inputs, this implies dimensionality reduction. The first layer from the input to the hidden layer acts as the encoder, and the values of the hidden units make up the code. The MLP is forced to find the best representation of the input in the hidden layer so as to be able to reproduce it again at the output layer. The encoder is written as where W are the parameters of the encoder. The second layer from the hidden units to the output units acts as the decoder, reconstructing the original signal from its encoded representation: where V are the parameters of the decoder. We use backpropagation to find the best encoder and decoder parameters so that the reconstruction error is minimized: In designing the encoder, we choose a code of small dimensionality and/or use an encoder of low capacity to force the encoder to preserve the most important characteristics of the data. The part that is discarded is due to noise or factors that are unimportant for the task. This is exactly the idea behind dimensionality reduction methods that we discussed in chapter 6 , and actually, it has been shown that an autoencoder MLP with one hidden layer of units ( i.e., a linear encoder) implements PCA ( Bourlard and Kamp 1 9 8 8 ) . Recall from section 6 .3 that PCA also minimizes the reconstruction error, the difference being that the H hidden unit weights are not the eigenvectors sorted in importance in terms of their eigenvalues, but they span the same space as the H principal eigenvectors. If the encoder and decoder are not one layer but each are MLPs with nonlinearity in the hidden units, the encoder implements nonlinear dimensionality reduction. In this latter case, we use networks that are inverses of each other architecturally, where typically the encoder compresses the data step by step in successive layers and the decoder expands it similarly step by step. We will talk more about such deep autoencoders in the next chapter, where we will see that this idea of an encoder and a decoder placed back to back and trained end to end, the encoder analyzing the input and converting it to a compressed intermediate representation and the decoder synthesizing the output from that, finds uses in many different applications. One interesting extension is the denoising autoencoder ( Vincent et al. 2 0 0 8 ) , where we add noise to create virtual examples: For any instance, the input to the encoder is noisy, but the required output of the decoder is noiseless. The noise is chosen to reflect whatever distortion one expects to see in the application; for example, in visual recognition, occlusions lead to missing inputs. The effect of giving noiseless and noisy versions of the same instance to the encoder with the same desired output is that the encoder learns to generate very similar embeddings for both because the same output needs to be generated from both, using the ( same) decoder. Another extension is the sparse autoencoder, where the aim is to learn embeddings that are longer dimensional but sparse ( Ranzato et al. 2 0 0 7 ) . The idea is that, if few of the code elements ( i.e., hidden unit activations) are nonzero, they will correspond to useful abstract properties of the instance ( so that the instance can be coded with a few of them) . To achieve this, we add a penalty term that penalizes nonzero elements of zt. Another way to use an MLP for dimensionality reduction is through multidimensional scaling ( see section 6 .7 ) . Mao and Jain ( 1 9 9 5 ) show how an MLP can be used to learn Sammon mapping. Recalling equation 6 .3 7 , Sammon stress is defined as An MLP with d inputs, H hidden units, and k < d output units is used to implement g( x|θ) , mapping the d-dimensional input to a k-dimensional vector, where θ corresponds to the weights of the MLP; of course, one can use more than one hidden layer if needed. Given a dataset of X = {xt}t, we can use gradient descent to minimize the Sammon stress directly to learn the MLP, namely, g( x|θ) , such that the distances between the k-dimensional representations are as close as possible to the distances in the original space. Note that in this case it is the output of the MLP that is the low-dimensional embedding, and not any of its hidden layer activations. It may also be a good idea at this point to remember the t-SNE algorithm for dimensionality reduction ( section 6 .1 3 ) that also uses gradient descent to solve an optimization problem based on the preservation of distances. 1 1 .1 1   Word2 vec Architecture In the noisy autoencoder, for two instances, one in its original form and one perturbed with noise, we specify the same original form as the output. This forces the encoder to generate similar codes for the two because the same output should be generated for both by the decoder. We can extend the idea to other contexts, still keeping the encoder-decoder structure: If for two different inputs we specify the same output, the encoder is forced to generate similar embeddings for the two. This is the idea behind the word2vec architecture ( Mikolov et al. 2 0 1 3 a) , where the output is a word and the input is its context, that is, the words that surround it. If two words frequently appear in the same context, they should be similar, and we will learn similar codes for them. The aim in word2 vec is to find a continuous representation for words that we can use in natural language processing applications, such as document classification. In the binary representation of words that underlies a bag of words ( see section 5 .7 ) , we first decide on a lexicon of d words that we believe are informative. To each word in the lexicon, we assign an integer index between 1 and d, and the representation of the word j is a d-dimensional vector of all zeros except 1 at element j. This representation has two major drawbacks: First, d is on the order of tens of thousands, and this increases the time and space complexity of the following model. The second and more critical problem here is that all words differ in two bits, so any relationship or similarity, semantic or syntactic, between words is not reflected in such a representation. There are two word2 vec models, CBOW and skip-gram. In both, we have an MLP with a d-dimensional input, d- dimensional output, and H < d hidden units in the hidden layer between them, and as such it resembles an autoencoder. Given a sentence and a center word, the input is the context and the output is the center word. The context uses a window that includes a number of words on both sides of the center word, for example, five on each side. The two models differ in the way they define the context. In CBOW, short for continuous bag of words, we average the binary representations of all the words in the window and that is given as input. That is, the d-dimensional input will have nonzero values for all the words that are part of the context. In skip-gram, we take the words in the context one at a time, and they form different training pairs where, again, the aim is to predict the center word. Thus, in skip-gram there is only one nonzero element in each input pair, but there will be multiple such pairs. For example, assume we have the sentence “Protesters in Paris clash with the French police.” and “Paris” as the center word. In CBOW, the input is the bag of words representation of [“Protesters”, “in”, “clash”, “with”, “the”, “French”, “police”] and the target is the bag of words representation of “Paris”. In skip-gram, this sentence generates seven training pairs; the first has “Protesters” as input and “Paris” as target, the second has “in” as input and “Paris” as target, the third has “clash” as input and “Paris” as target, up until the last one, which has “police” as input and “Paris” as target. The center word slides, and all words in the sentence get to be the center word, which means we also have the same instances again with the input and output swapped. In practice, skip-gram is found to work better and is used more frequently than CBOW. Note that the order of the words in the sentence is lost in both CBOW and skip-gram. In both, as output, we predict a word. As such, word2 vec solves a classification problem with d classes; the aim is to choose the class that corresponds to the center word, so we use softmax activations at the output, and we minimize the cross-entropy. For any word j, when the corresponding input xj is set to 1 , the H-dimensional vector of activations at the hidden layer, namely, z, is its code; note that because all other inputs are 0 , this will be equal to the H outgoing weights of xj. The code is said to be continuous or distributed; there will be many nonzero values. It is also called a word embedding in the sense that this is the low-dimensional representation of the input, and as such, this can be viewed as dimensionality reduction from d to H. Typically, d is on the order of tens of thousands or more whereas H is on the order of hundreds. There are a number of ways in which word2 vec can be improved. Words such as “the” or “with” that appear too frequently can be used fewer times than they actually appear. Note that, unlike with bag of words, they are not omitted; they are needed to learn relationships. Similarly, context words that are far from the center word can be sampled fewer times than words that are close. Such decisions, as well as the size of the context window, depend on the language. Computation time can be decreased by sampling at the output. Remember that we have d outputs where d is at least on the order of tens of thousands, and we need to calculate all of them to calculate the denominator of the softmax. Still, most of them will be very close to zero, so instead of all, one can just randomly choose a small number of them, typically 1 0 –2 0 , and calculate the outputs for only those, assuming that all the rest will be zero; this is called negative sampling ( Mikolov et al. 2 0 1 3 b) . The reason that word2 vec learns good word embeddings is because of the way the task is defined. If we have two words that frequently appear in the same context, that is, frequently surrounded by the same words, they need to be coded similarly so that the same words can be decoded from both. It is also critical that the network is simple; with a network with many hidden layers there would be the risk of memorizing pairs, but with a simple network, every example leaves a small trace and those accumulate to define codes that work well overall. Consider sentences where there is the word “Paris”. It is very likely that we also have sentences in our corpus that are very similar, with “London” ( or any other city) in the place of “Paris”. So we will have training examples with “London” or “Paris” as the input with the same outputs, and this will result in similar codes to be learned for the two; actually, we expect to see cities clustered in some part of the H-dimensional space, encoding this semantic similarity in the code. Using a similar argument, we can also expect “Paris” and “Parisian” to be closely located but along other dimensions of the code or, for example, “see” and “seeing” or “saw” to be nearby, in these cases indicating a syntactic similarity. This holds for learning general relationships. In the example sentence above we have the pair “Paris” and “French”, and we expect to see this pair in many sentences in many different ( ideally more peaceful) contexts, which will place them nearby in the code space. Furthermore, we also expect to see quite similar sentences but this time with “London” and “English” instead of “Paris” and “French”. So not only will we have “Paris” and “London”, and “French” and “English” nearby in different parts of the space, but the position of “Paris” with respect to “French” is expected to be very similar to the position of “London” with respect to “English”. Let us say Vec( w) denotes the H-dimensional code vector for word w. If we calculate Vec( “French”) − Vec( “Paris”) + Vec( “London”) , we expect to be close to Vec( “English”) ; we expect Vec( “French”) − Vec( “Paris”) and Vec( “English”) − Vec( “London”) to be similar vectors ( see figure 1 1 .1 6 ) . Of course, this will not hold exactly because we do not have the exact same sentences or an equal number of examples for each in our training corpus, but if we have enough of them, such relationships will be reflected in the codes approximately. See Mikolov et al. ( 2 0 1 3 a, 2 0 1 3 b) for other examples. There are a number of extensions to the basic word2 vec model. There are, for example, variants that work at the subword level of character sequences or at the higher level of sentences or paragraphs. There are also other methods to learn word embeddings, such as GloVe ( Pennington, Socher, and Manning 2 0 1 4 ) and fastText ( Bojanowski et al. 2 0 1 7 ) , which in certain cases may work better than word2 vec. The word2 vec approach is also interesting in the sense that an auxiliary supervised task is created to solve the original unsupervised task. Learning an embedding of words is an unsupervised problem, but the task of predicting a word from its context is a supervised task. The data for the original problem has no labels, but when it is recast as a prediction problem, it is reorganized with labels, and a supervised classifier is trained on it. We will see another example of this with the generative adversarial networks in chapter 1 2 . Figure 1 1 .1 6 Word2 vec example ( hypothetical) . In the code space, because of similarities of context, cities are expected to form one cluster, adjectives denoting the country of origin form another cluster, and the position of one with respect to other is expected to be preserved for both pairs. We expect Vec( “French”) − Vec( “Paris”) and Vec( “English”) − Vec( “London”) to be similar vectors, so that for example, Vec( “French”) − Vec( “Paris”) + Vec( “London”) is expected to be close to Vec( “English”) . 1 1 .1 2   Notes Research on artificial neural networks is as old as the digital computer. McCulloch and Pitts ( 1 9 4 3 ) proposed the first mathematical model for the artificial neuron. Rosenblatt ( 1 9 6 2 ) proposed the perceptron model and a learning algorithm. Minsky and Papert ( 1 9 6 9 ) showed the limitation of single-layer perceptrons, for example, the XOR problem, and since there was no algorithm to train an MLP with a hidden layer at that time, the work on artificial neural networks almost stopped except at a few places. The renaissance of neural networks came with the paper by Hopfield ( 1 9 8 2 ) . This was followed by the two-volume parallel distributed processing ( PDP) book written by the PDP Research Group ( Rumelhart, McClelland, and the PDP Research Group 1 9 8 6 ) . It seems as though backpropagation was invented independently in several places almost at the same time, and the limitation of a single-layer perceptron no longer held. Starting in the mid-1 9 8 0 s, there has been a huge explosion of work on artificial neural network models from various disciplines: physics, statistics, psychology, cognitive science, neuroscience, and linguistics, not to mention computer science, electrical engineering, and adaptive control. Perhaps the most important contribution of research on artificial neural networks is this synergy that bridged various disciplines, especially statistics and engineering. It is thanks to this that the field of machine learning is now well established. There are various early textbooks on artificial neural networks that are still readable: Hertz, Krogh, and Palmer ( 1 9 9 1 ) is the earliest and has the physicist viewpoint. Bishop ( 1 9 9 5 ) has a pattern recognition emphasis. We can say that starting with neural networks, computer scientists who work on AI discovered the importance of statistics and started to learn it. As a very recent source, Goodfellow, Bengio, and Courville ( 2 0 1 6 ) discuss the training of neural networks and provide a separate chapter on autoencoders. Artificial neural networks lost their popularity in the mid- 1 9 9 0 s, when because of limited computing power and small data sets they were limited in what they could learn. Despite such constraints, however, there were impressive applications even then, which were harbingers of the success of today’s deep neural networks. Tesauro’s TD-Gammon program ( Tesauro 1 9 9 4 ) used reinforcement learning ( see chapter 1 9 ) to train an MLP that played backgammon at a master level. Pomerleau’s ALVINN was a neural network that autonomously drove a van up to 2 0 miles per hour after learning by observing a driver for five minutes ( Pomerleau 1 9 9 1 ) . LeCun et al. ( 1 9 8 9 ) trained a convolutional neural network to learn handwritten checks. Artificial neural networks became popular again around the 2 0 1 0 s under the name “deep learning.” As we will see in the next chapter, the basics are not that much different, and not much is new theoretically. The main change is that in the last two decades computing has gotten so much cheaper, and nowadays we have parallel processors and cloud servers. We also have much larger data sets. The upshot is that today we can build much larger networks with many layers and train them on much larger data sets, which has resulted in successful applications in many diverse areas, from face recognition to playing Go. There are a number of software packages and libraries for training neural network models, and they make the task of defining and training deep networks with many layers and units very easy. Some of them also support parallel hardware and can thus make learning very efficient. Before using those, however, it is recommended very strongly that you write the code for simple networks yourself. For example, for simple tasks such as learning XOR ( figure 1 1 .7 ) and one-dimensional regression ( figure 1 1 .1 0 ) , it is a very good idea to write the code and to run it visualizing how the parameters change as learning proceeds. How the network output and hidden unit activations change, for example, will enhance your intuition about the role of such hyperparameters as the number of hidden units and learning factor. In this chapter, we continue with deep neural networks composed of many hidden layers. We discuss how such models can be trained efficiently, different deep network architectures, and some applications where they are used successfully. 1 2 .1    Introduction WHEN A linear model is not sufficient, one possibility is to define new features that are nonlinear functions of the input, for example, higher-order terms, and then build a linear model in the space of those features; we discussed this in section 1 0 .2 . This requires us to know what such good basis functions are. Another possibility is to use one of the feature extraction methods we discussed in chapter 6 to learn the new space, for example, PCA or Isomap; such methods have the advantage that they are trained on data, but they are generally unsupervised. Currently the best approach seems to be to use a multilayer perceptron ( MLP) that extracts such features in its hidden layer, as we discussed in chapter 1 1 . The MLP has the advantage that the first layer ( feature extraction) and the second layer ( where those features are combined to predict the final output) are learned together in a supervised manner. In chapter 1 1 , we introduced the basic perceptron with a single layer and the MLP with one hidden layer. Though we know that the MLP with one hidden layer is a universal approximator; that is, it can approximate any function with arbitrary accuracy, it may need a very large number of hidden units to achieve that. It has long been known empirically that a “long and thin” network not only has fewer parameters ( and hence smaller complexity) than a “short and fat” one but also achieves better generalization. This is the idea behind deep neural networks, where we networks have many hidden layers and, starting from the raw input, each hidden layer combines the values in its preceding layer and learns more complicated functions of the input. Successive hidden layers correspond to more abstract representations until we get to the final layer, where the outputs are learned in terms of these most abstract concepts. For example, we will see the convolutional neural network for image recognition in section 1 2 .5 , where, starting from local group of pixels, we get to edges, then to corners, and so on, until we get to a digit. We know that an image is composed of such primitives at different levels, and we use this knowledge to define the connectivity and the overall architecture. If we used an MLP where each hidden unit is connected to all the inputs, the network has no knowledge that the inputs are face images, or even that the input is two- dimensional. Using a convolutional network where hidden units are fed with localized two-dimensional patches in the image is an inductive bias and as such is a way to feed this information of local correlations such that correct abstractions can be learned at different levels. In deep learning, the idea is to learn feature levels of increasing abstraction with minimum human contribution ( Bengio 2 0 0 9 ; Goodfellow, Bengio, and Courville 2 0 1 6 ) . This is because in most applications, we do not know what structure there is in the input, or we may know it only in the first few layers of basic feature extraction, and any dependencies there are should be automatically discovered during training. It is this extraction of dependencies, or patterns, or regularities, that allows abstraction and learning general descriptions. Though deep learning is attractive, it has various potential problems. First, a deep network is much larger, with more weights and processing units, and hence needs more memory and more computation; luckily, GPUs and multicore architectures are getting cheaper every day, which helps us with that. Second, a deep network has more free parameters, and training it is more difficult. Not only do we have a more complicated error surface, but the fact that there are many hidden layers is also problematic. For example, in backpropagating the error to an early layer, because of the chain rule we multiply the derivatives in all the layers afterward, and the gradient may vanish or explode. This has led to many heuristics to finetune the basic gradient descent method, and we will discuss those in section 1 2 .3 . Finetuning the network architecture and connectivity is also useful, as we will see in section 1 2 .6 . The old approach was to train one layer at a time ( Hinton and Salakhutdinov 2 0 0 6 ) . The aim of each layer is to extract the salient features in the data fed to it, and a method such as the autoencoder that we discussed in section 1 1 .9 can be used for this purpose; there is the extra advantage that we can use unlabeled data for this purpose. So, starting from the raw input, we train an autoencoder, and the encoded representation learned in its hidden layer is then used as input to train the next autoencoder, and so on, until we get to the final layer that is trained in a supervised manner with the labeled data. Once all the layers are trained in this way, one by one, they are all stacked, and the whole network is finetuned with the labeled data. Today, with more computing power and labeled data available, the whole deep network can be trained in a supervised manner. Still, using an unsupervised method to initialize the weights may sometimes work better than random initialization—learning can be done much faster and with fewer labeled data. Or, earlier feature extraction layers can be “transferred” from another network trained on a larger but similar data. Deep learning methods are attractive mainly because they need less manual interference. We do not need to craft the right features or suitable basis functions or kernels ( chapter 1 4 ) , or worry about optimizing the exact network architecture. Once we have data—and these days we have “big” data—and sufficient computation available, we just wait and let the learning algorithm discover by itself all that is necessary. The idea of multiple layers of increasing abstraction that lies underneath deep learning is intuitive. Not only in vision— in handwritten digits or face images—but in many applications, we can think of layers of abstraction, and discovering such abstract representations allows a better description of the problem. Consider machine translation. For example, starting with an English sentence, which is a sequence of characters, in multiple levels of processing and abstraction that are learned automatically from a very large corpus of English sentences to code the lexical, syntactic, and semantic rules of the English language, we would get to the most abstract representation. Now consider the same sentence in French. The levels of processing learned this time from a French corpus would be different, but if two sentences mean the same thing, at the most abstract, language-independent level, they should have very similar representations. So we can view machine translation as basically composed of an encoder and a decoder back to back. The encoder takes an English sentence and generates a language-independent embedding of the meaning, and a decoder takes this and synthesizes the corresponding French sentence. Training is done end to end; the training data contains pairs of English and French sentences, and all intermediate processing is learned. That is, all the lexical, syntactic, and semantic constraints that are necessary for analysis and synthesis are learned from data and implemented in the many layers of the deep encoder and decoder networks. This is basically how state-of-the-art machine translation is learned and done ( Wu et al. 2 0 1 6 ) . We are familiar with this type of processing in computer science; this is, for example, how a compiler works: There is the front end that does lexical and syntactic analyses and generates an intermediate representation, and the back end takes this as input and generates code for a particular processor. One can adapt the compiler to different languages and processors by changing only the front or back end, respectively. We have many other examples of the same approach in machine learning as well. For example, consider the task of generating captions for images ( Vinyals et al. 2 0 1 5 ) . The encoder takes the image as input, analyzes it in a deep network, and generates an embedding which is an abstract representation of the image content; the decoder takes this and generates an English sentence as the caption. We also see this in game playing, for example, in the Atari player ( Mnih et al. 2 0 1 3 ) . The encoder takes the screen image and generates a compressed embedding, and the decoder takes this and decides on the action. Again, the whole network is trained end to end. Previously, such a system would be handled in two stages: There would be one vision module taking an image and generating an intermediate representation, and there would be an action module taking the intermediate representation and deciding the action; the two modules would typically be designed by different groups of people with different areas of expertise who would sit down together and decide on the intermediate representation. Now with deep, end-to-end training, the two modules are trained in a coupled manner; our training data consists of pairs of input at the very beginning and the output at the very end, for example, pairs of an image and the best action, and it is the learning algorithm that decides on the intermediate representation. All we need is a large enough network and lots and lots of data to cover as many combinations as possible. Let us now see how this is done. 1 2 .2    How to Train Multiple Hidden Layers 1 2 .2 .1    Rectified Linear Unit In chapter 1 1 , we used sigmoid and tanh as nonlinear activation functions. An activation function for hidden units that has become popular recently with deep networks is the rectified linear unit ( ReLU) ( Nair and Hinton 2 0 1 0 ; Glorot, Bordes, and Bengio 2 0 1 1 ) , which is defined as Though ReLU is not differentiable at a = 0 , we use it anyway; we use the left derivative: One advantage of ReLU is that, because it does not saturate ( unlike sigmoid and tanh) , updates can still be done for large positive a. The other advantage is that, for some inputs, some hidden unit activations will be zero, meaning that we will have a sparse representation. Sparse representations lead to faster training ( where there are fewer nonzero hidden units, there is less interference between them) ; they are also easier to interpret. The disadvantage of ReLU is that, because the derivative is zero for a ≤ 0 , there is no further training if, for a hidden unit, the weighted sum somehow becomes negative. This implies that one should be careful in initializing the weights so that the initial activation for all hidden units is positive. In the leaky ReLU ( Maas, Hannun, and Ng 2 0 1 3 ) , the output is also linear on the negative side but with a smaller slope, just enough to make sure that there will be updates for negative activations, albeit small: For example, α is taken as 0 .0 1 , which is the derivative for a ≤ 0 . 1 2 .2 .2    Initialization One should be careful when initializing the weights in a deep network. In chapter 1 1 , we said that we can choose initial weight values uniformly randomly from the interval [−0 .0 1 , 0 .0 1 ], and when we have an application with tens of inputs and hidden units, this is sufficient. If a unit is receiving inputs from thousands of units or more, the range should be scaled down correspondingly. The aim is always to make sure that we start with activations where the derivative is nonzero. In the case of sigmoid and tanh, the derivative is maximum at zero, so we need to initialize so that we get small values and so that we do not accidentally get a value less than −5 or greater than 5 . For ReLU, we need to make sure that we get a nonnegative value; for example, initially weights can similarly be very close to zero and we can have a positive bias. 1 2 .2 .3    Generalizing Backpropagation to Multiple Hidden Layers In chapter 1 1 , we derived the update equations for a multilayer perceptron with a single hidden layer. It is simple. It is also local; that is, the change in a weight uses only the values of the presynaptic and postsynaptic units ( the units before and after the connection) and the error ( suitably backpropagated) . When online training is used, it does not need to store the training set and can adapt as the task to be learned changes. But by itself, gradient descent converges slowly. Methods such as the conjugate gradient and second-order methods are computationally intensive and can not be used easily with deep networks with many weights ( Goodfellow, Bengio, and Courville 2 0 1 6 ) . However, simple techniques improve the performance of the gradient descent considerably, making it feasible in real applications. 1 2 .3 .1    Momentum Let us say that wi is any weight in an MLP in any layer, including the biases. At each parameter update, successive gradient values may be so different that large oscillations may occur and slow convergence. t is the time index that is the epoch number in batch learning and the iteration number in online or minibatch learning. The idea is to take a running average by incorporating the previous update in the current change as if there is a momentum due to previous updates. For each weight wi, we keep an additional value si, originally zero, that keeps a running average of the past gradients, and that is how much we update: The hyperparameter 0 < α < 1 is the decay or forgetting parameter of the running average and is generally taken as 0 .9 . Momentum is especially useful when online or minibatch learning is used, where as a result we get an effect of averaging and smooth the trajectory during convergence. The disadvantage is that the si values should be stored in extra memory. 1 2 .3 .2    Adaptive Learning Factor In gradient descent, the learning factor η determines the magnitude of change to be made in the parameter. Typically it takes a value less than or equal to 0 .2 . A very early heuristic was to make it adaptive for faster convergence, where it is kept large when learning takes place and is decreased when learning slows down: Thus we increase η by a constant amount ( or keep it unchanged) if the error on the training set decreases and decrease it geometrically if it increases. Because E may oscillate from one epoch to another, it is a better idea to take the average of the past few epochs as Et. In a deep network with many hidden layers and units, the contributions of weights to the error are not the same, and one can adapt the learning factor separately for each weight, depending on convergence along that direction. The idea in such methods is to accumulate the past error gradient magnitudes for each weight and then make the learning factor inversely proportional to that. In directions where the gradient is small, the learning factor is larger to compensate, and it can be smaller along directions where the gradient is already large. In AdaGrad ( Duchi, Hazan, and Singer 2 0 1 1 ) , we keep a running sum of all the past gradients; in RMSProp ( Hinton 2 0 1 2 ) , we keep a running average where we give more importance to more recent values.
